strengths: BiAlign proposes a clear, relevant extension to knowledge distillation: align teacher and student preferences over demonstration subsets alongside token-level output distributions. It targets an important aspect of in-context learning without adding inference overhead.

The central empirical result is supported across several settings. Average performance improves over Output-Align from 29.2 to 30.2 with the 13B teacher and from 30.0 to 31.7 with the 70B teacher. Experiments with Phi models and a larger student provide additional evidence of transferability.

The computational controls are valuable. The paper acknowledges approximately 2.3 times greater training cost and tests both additional subset data for Output-Align and shorter BiAlign training. These comparisons support an advantage beyond simply using more computation or training inputs.

The equations, algorithm, major hyperparameters, and extensive ablations make the core method understandable and provide a reasonable basis for reproduction. Held-out preference agreement also supports the narrower claim that the ranking objective transfers some teacher preferences.
weaknesses: Statistical reliability is insufficiently characterized: run counts, seeds, and uncertainty estimates are absent despite stochastic training and subset sampling. HumanEval improvements over Vanilla amount to roughly one or two additional solved problems. Its FT and C-Pretrain scores of 14.2 and 13.2 also require clarification: neither corresponds to a single greedy evaluation on 164 problems, and any averaging protocol is unspecified.

Exact replication would benefit from additional implementation details. No code or configuration artifact is linked, and sequence truncation, loss reductions, numerical handling of the range denominator in Equation 3, and QLoRA settings are unspecified. Loss reductions are particularly relevant to interpreting the reported ranking-loss weight.

The mechanism is only partially established. Figure 4 measures agreement on the highest- and lowest-scoring subsets, rather than full ranking agreement or a causal connection to downstream gains. Because subsets vary in demonstration count, the analysis does not distinguish preferences for demonstration content from preferences for context length. Comparisons among equal-sized subsets would strengthen this interpretation.

The comparisons establish improvements over the implemented forward-KL baseline, but broader superiority over existing distillation approaches remains untested. The paper cites other relevant distillation methods without evaluating them. Moreover, the simpler alternative ranking loss performs comparably, so the evidence favors the general preference-alignment strategy more strongly than the particular proposed loss.

Claims about preferentially improving complex reasoning exceed the evidence. Relative gains across four different math datasets do not control for baseline accuracy, task format, or difficulty, and isolated reasoning examples cannot establish a general mechanism. The controlled benchmark improvements support a Findings recommendation, while these evidential and comparative limits weaken the case for main-conference acceptance.
